In the student council room after school, the whiteboard was already full: logins, star ratings, comments, a dark theme, a search bar. Sarika capped the marker.
“Okay, stop. If we build all this, when do we launch?”
Asif counted on his fingers. “Maybe March?”
“And pre-boards are in January. The people who need notes need them before that.” She wiped half the board. “So what's the smallest thing that's still useful? Someone from Class Ten opens a page, clicks Chemistry, gets the PDFs. That's it.”
“No logins? Then anyone could upload rubbish.”
“So for now only we upload. People send us their notes, we check them and put them up.”
Asif frowned, then wrote VERSION 1 at the top: one page, PDFs under each subject. Below a line, smaller: Later: accounts, ratings.
“We could have that up by next Friday,” he said.

qa.q: When are the pre-boards, according to Sarika?
qa.a: In January.

qa.a: She is worried the long feature list will push the launch past the pre-boards, and feels impatient to get something useful to students first.

qa.q: What else could help the team decide what goes into version one?
qa.a: Asking a few Class Ten students what they need most, so the first page matches real demand rather than guesses.

qa.q: How might a Class Ten student looking for notes see this plan?
qa.a: They get chemistry PDFs before pre-boards without signing up, which matters far more to them than ratings.

Hi Kashish,
I've been thinking about Saturday's meeting, and I want to argue for something before we start building. Please read to the end before replying!
Our list has twelve features. Your login page design looks great, honestly. But if we build all twelve, the notes site will be ready after the exams it's meant for. So I asked myself: what is the least we can put online that still helps someone on Monday? My answer is one page with subject headings (Physics, Chemistry, Maths, Biology) and the PDFs people have already shared with us listed under each. No accounts, no ratings, no comments.
Then we watch. If people use it and ask for logins, your design goes in next. If nobody opens it, we've lost a week, not a term.
Can we talk about this at lunch tomorrow?
Tushar

subtype: Approach: task decomposition and dividing roles [Action]
passage:
Project supervisor's note, Class Nine website project, week four
When this group started, Joseph, Vaibhav and Noor were all “doing everything”, which meant three people editing the same homepage and nobody writing content. In week two I asked them to list every task. They came back with a shared sheet: design (Noor), content (Vaibhav), coding (Joseph), each task with a name and a date beside it. They also fixed two ten-minute check-ins, Tuesdays and Fridays at lunch, standing by the lab door.
I have watched three of those check-ins. They are quick: done, stuck, next. On Friday Vaibhav admitted the history page was late; Joseph offered a simpler layout so it could go in as plain text first.
The site is not finished, but for the first time every page has an owner. I will look at their sheet again next Friday before suggesting anything.

qa.q: When are the group's ten-minute check-ins?
qa.a: Tuesdays and Fridays at lunch, standing by the lab door.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav have felt admitting the history page was late?
qa.a: Vaibhav was probably a little embarrassed, but safe enough to say it, since the check-in is built for "stuck" as well as "done" 😅

qa.q: What could the group try if a task's owner falls ill before a due date?
qa.a: Use the Tuesday check-in to hand that task to whoever is ahead and move its date on the sheet, so the plan stays honest.

qa.q: How does the new split look from Joseph's side?
qa.a: Joseph can focus on coding without three people fighting over the homepage, and can spot a way to help when content runs late.

grounding: Shows three teens splitting a website into design, content and coding on a shared sheet with owners and dates, and checking in twice a week for ten minutes.

Wednesday
First real meeting for the society notice-board site. Divyansh wanted to start coding right away, Arham wanted to pick colours, and I wanted to write the events list. So we did the boring thing first. On the shared sheet we wrote every job: home page layout, event list, photos, contact form, testing on phones. Then three columns: who, what, by when.
Me: event list and notices, by Sunday. Arham: design and photos, by Saturday. Divyansh: building the pages, by next Wednesday. Monday and Thursday, ten minutes after tuition, we check the sheet together. Ten minutes only, Divyansh set a timer 😅
Felt slow tonight. But when Divyansh asked, “Where's the event list?”, I could say “Sunday, see row four” and nobody argued. That never happened on our science project.
– Tejas

subtype: Approach: using free tools within constraints [Thinking]
passage:
Last year I built a site for our colony's book exchange, and the first thing I learned was what zero rupees buys. I'm Dhruv. No card, no pocket money to spare, so I used a site builder that costs nothing, with hosting that was free too. That plan allowed five pages and no search box.
Jatin, who helped me collect the lists, kept saying, “Without search, nobody will use it.” I nearly gave up. Then I thought: five pages, fine. One page each for Classes Eight to Twelve. If each page is short and sorted, people don't need search; they need a clean list.
So I spent my effort there, checking every title twice and removing books already given away. The limit became my rule: nothing goes on a page unless someone can pick it up this week. By June, forty-one books had changed hands.

qa.q: How many pages did the free plan allow?
qa.a: The free plan allowed five pages.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when Jatin kept saying nobody would use it without search?
qa.a: Dhruv felt discouraged enough to nearly give up, until the reasoning about short, sorted lists brought back some confidence.

qa.q: What else could Dhruv have tried if the lists grew too long for one page per class?
qa.a: Split each class page by subject within the same five pages, or ask users what they look for first before adding anything.

qa.q: How might Jatin see the site after forty-one books changed hands?
qa.a: Jatin would probably admit a clean list worked without search, and feel part of the success after collecting the lists.

grounding: Shows a teen with no money using a free builder and hosting, accepting no search box and turning the page limit into a rule about content quality.

subtype: Approach: testing with real users early [Action]
passage:
When my recipe blog had just three pages, I did something that felt too early: I showed it to five relatives at Nani's house one Sunday. I'm Samir, and the blog was meant to collect our family's Konkani dishes.
I didn't explain anything. I handed my phone to each person and said, “Find the fish curry.” Then I just watched and wrote in a notebook.
Saurabh Mama went straight to About and got lost. Nani kept pressing the photo, thinking it was a button. Two of my aunts scrolled to the bottom looking for a menu that was hidden behind three little lines at the top. Only my cousin found it in under a minute.
That night I didn't add a single recipe. I put the menu as plain words across the top, made the photos open the recipe, and sent it to Saurabh Mama again. He found the curry in seconds.

qa.q: What did Samir ask each person to find?
qa.a: The fish curry.

qa.q: What might Samir have felt watching Nani press the photo like a button?
qa.a: Samir was probably surprised and a little embarrassed, but also curious, since each wrong tap showed where the blog confused people.

qa.q: What other approach could have found the same problems, and would it work as well?
qa.a: Asking relatives what they thought would mostly get polite praise; watching them try a task shows real confusion, so watching works better.

qa.q: What was the first version like for Saurabh Mama?
qa.a: It was confusing: he went to About and got lost, but after the fix he found the curry in seconds.

grounding: Shows a student watching five relatives use a rough recipe blog, noting where they get lost, and fixing the menu before adding more.

Coach's notes, club family day, Saturday
Karthik brought five relatives to test his blog of the snacks his family's tea stall sells, and I watched from the next table. He gave each person one task, “find how to make the banana fritters”, and stayed silent while they tried.
His grandfather's brother, Jomon, tapped the logo three times, expecting a menu. His mother and two cousins scrolled past the recipe list because it sat below a long welcome paragraph. Only his aunt found it quickly. Karthik wrote down each stuck point and how long it took.
Afterwards he didn't open his list of new recipes. He moved the recipe list to the top, cut the welcome to two lines, and made the logo lead home. Before the session ended, Jomon tried again and found the fritters in under a minute. Next week I will suggest testing with classmates too.

qa.q: What task did Karthik give each relative?
qa.a: To find how to make the banana fritters.

qa.q: What might Karthik have felt while noting each stuck point?
qa.a: He was probably a bit deflated at first, but also focused and eager, since each stuck point showed exactly what to fix.

qa.q: What could Karthik try next to check the fix?
qa.a: Test with a few classmates who have never seen the blog, since relatives may already know how the family names its snacks.

qa.q: How was the first version for Jomon?
qa.a: For Jomon it was frustrating to tap the logo three times with nothing happening, but after the fix the fritters took under a minute.

grounding: A coach notes a student watching five relatives try his recipe blog, recording where they get stuck, and fixing navigation before adding recipes.

subtype: Approach: overbuilding features before anyone uses it [Pitfall]
passage:
Class teacher's note, end of term
In July Nirmala told me she was building an app so our class could check the timetable. Parul had asked for exactly that; the printed sheet on the board kept getting torn.
By August Nirmala was showing me a chat room inside the app. By September, badges for logging in every day, and a night theme she redesigned twice. Each time I asked, “Can the class see the timetable yet?” she said, “Not until it's complete.”
The exam-free weeks ended in October. She has not touched it since, and nothing was ever shared. Last week Parul simply photographed the timetable and posted it in the class group. Forty-two people reacted to the photo.
Nirmala saw it. She looked flat for the rest of the day. I have asked her to show me just the timetable screen next term, nothing else, and put it out as it is.

qa.q: What did Parul post in the class group?
qa.a: A photograph of the timetable.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's flat look suggest after seeing the photo?
qa.a: It suggests she felt deflated and a little foolish, seeing a simple photo meet the need her unfinished app never reached.

qa.q: Which approach would have suited the class better in July?
qa.a: Share just a timetable page first, then ask classmates which extras they want, so building follows real use.

qa.q: How did those months look to Parul?
qa.a: Parul wanted an easy way to see the timetable, waited for an app that never came, and in the end solved it with a photo.

grounding: Shows a teen adding chat, badges and a night theme before sharing, running out of free weeks, and launching nothing while the class wanted a timetable.

Sunday night, 11:40
Exams start in nine days, which means the app is officially on hold. Again.
Honest list of what it has: custom avatars, a leaderboard, points for finishing homework, sounds when you tick a task, and a settings page with nothing to set. What it doesn't have: a single person using it.
Akash asked in June for one thing: a page with the week's tuition homework, because Sir's messages get buried. One page. I said, “Give me two weeks.” Then I thought, if I'm doing it, let's do it properly, and started on the leaderboard.
Today in the tuition group Akash wrote, “Anyone know what's due Tuesday? 😩” and six people replied with different answers. I nearly typed “my app would fix this”. It wouldn't. It isn't out.
After exams: one page first. Nothing else.
– Vidya

subtype: Approach: pre-mortem on why the project might die [Thinking]

“Before we write a single line, try this,” Rehana said, pulling the laptop closer in the canteen. “It's two months from now. Our lost-and-found site is dead. Nobody updates it. Why?”
Harsha laughed. “Because it's us?”
“Seriously. Reasons.”
“Okay... unit tests in September. We all stop.”
“Good. Next.”
“Honestly? You'd end up doing everything, and when you get busy, it dies.”
Rehana winced, then typed it. “That's probably the real one. Third?”
“We get bored. It's not exciting after launch.”
“So: tests, one-person project, boredom.” She tapped the screen. “Tests are on the calendar, so we plan a two-week pause and tell people. For the one-person problem, each of us owns a section; you take the found-items page. Boredom... once a month we check if anyone's using it. If not, we fix it or stop honestly.”
Harsha nodded. “Okay. I'm in, for real this time.”

qa.q: Which page does Harsha take?
qa.a: The found-items page.

qa.q: Why did Rehana wince when Harsha named the second reason?
qa.a: Rehana felt a sting of recognition, since doing everything alone was probably the real risk, but was glad it was said aloud before starting.

qa.q: What else could the team add to the plan from this exercise?
qa.a: Keep the reasons and fixes where both can see them and revisit them at the monthly check, to see which risks are actually showing up.

qa.q: How might the plan feel to Harsha after this talk?
qa.a: Harsha has real ownership and a planned pause for tests, so joining feels safer and more serious, "for real this time".

subtype: Approach: pre-mortem on why the project might die [Thinking]
passage:
The best ten minutes of our project happened before we built anything. I'm Dhruv. Last year Leela and I, plus two others from the eco club, wanted a site where students could sign up to water the school garden.
It was August. Leela said, “Let's pretend it's October and the site is abandoned. Why did it die?” It felt gloomy, but we did it. We came up with three answers: half-yearly exams in September, only one of us knowing how to update it, and everyone losing interest once it stopped being new.
So we changed the plan on the spot. We marked the exam weeks on the calendar as a planned pause, with a notice on the site. All four of us learned to update the sign-up sheet, not just me. And we added a “garden of the month” photo to keep it fun.
It lasted until March. Not forever, but long past October.

qa.q: How many answers did the group come up with for why the site died?
qa.a: Three answers.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel about Leela's exercise at first, and later?
qa.a: Dhruv found it gloomy at first, then felt relieved and a little proud, because naming the risks led to the planned pause and shared updating 😊

qa.q: Which other approach could the eco club have combined with this exercise?
qa.a: A monthly look at how many students signed up, so a slow decline would show early and could be fixed before the site died.

qa.q: How might Leela see the site lasting until March?
qa.a: Leela would likely feel the gloomy exercise was worth it, since the risks named that day were the ones they avoided.

grounding: Shows a team imagining its garden sign-up site abandoned two months later, naming exams, one-person upkeep and lost interest, and planning around them.

I'm Manjula, and I sit two rows behind Mahima, so I watched her class-website plan unfold. On Monday she went desk to desk with a printed list of our names and a question: “Can I put your photo on the class page? Yes, no, or only in a group?” She ticked each answer. Three people said no. She crossed their names off the photo list without arguing.
On Tuesday I noticed she'd changed the captions: first names only, no surnames, no school name at the top, no mention of which bus stop we use.
On Wednesday she took her laptop to Mrs Pillai, our class teacher, and I saw them scroll through it together. Mrs Pillai pointed at something, and Mahima blurred one photo where a house number showed behind two kids.
The site went up on Friday. I checked. My photo was in the group one, like I'd asked.

qa.a: Yes, no, or only in a group.

qa.a: It suggests she felt the refusals were fair and was comfortable, even respectful, about them, putting classmates' choice above having more photos.

qa.q: What else could Mahima do to keep the site safe over time?
qa.a: Share the link only within the class and ask again before adding any new photos.

qa.q: How does the finished site feel to Manjula?
qa.a: Manjula feels respected, since the photo appeared exactly as asked, only in the group one.

Monday: Lalremsiami has a draft of the girls' football team site ready: full names, shirt numbers, photos, and the time of every Saturday practice at the ground. Dear Samir bhai,
You asked how my online stall went. Honestly: badly, and it's my own fault.
I finished the site in May. Twenty hand-painted bookmarks, photos taken on the terrace in good light, a simple order form. I was so proud of it that I just waited. I thought people would find it, because it was online and anyone could see it.
Three weeks later, the visit counter said nine. Four of those were me checking.
I never told my class. I never showed the neighbourhood group or the aunties who run the Sunday craft fair. I spent all my planning on making it and none on telling anyone it existed. The bookmarks are still in a shoebox.
Could you tell me how you got the first customers for your tiffin service? I think I need to start there, not with a new design.
Farhan

qa.q: What did the visit counter say after three weeks?
qa.a: It said nine, and four of those were Farhan checking.

qa.q: How does Farhan seem to feel writing this letter?
qa.a: Farhan feels disappointed and a bit ashamed, calling it "my own fault", but also ready to learn 😔

qa.q: What could Farhan try first to find visitors?
qa.a: Tell the class, share the link in the neighbourhood group and ask to show the bookmarks at the Sunday craft fair, since people only come if they know.

qa.q: How might Samir bhai read this letter?
qa.a: Samir bhai may recognise a common first mistake and be glad Farhan is asking about customers rather than redesigning again.

grounding: Shows a student finishing a small online stall and waiting for visitors who never come, because there was no plan to tell anyone.

subtype: Approach: assuming visitors will just arrive [Pitfall]
passage:
You asked about my uniform-swap store, Binita, so okay, here's the embarrassing version. I'm Rashmi, the girl who built a whole online shop and then sat there waiting.
It was a good idea! Families outgrow uniforms every year, and new ones cost a lot. I photographed twenty sets, listed the sizes, and made a page to ask for one. It took the whole summer holiday. Then I launched it and... nothing. Week one, zero requests. Week two, one, from my own aunt, who felt sorry for me.
I kept refreshing the page as if people would just appear. They didn't, because nobody knew it existed. I never put up a notice at school, never asked the parents' group, never told the tailor near the gate who sees every family in June.
Next June I'm doing the telling part first, before I take a single photo.

subtype: Approach: iterating from feedback and usage numbers [Revision]

The inter-school science fair was on Saturday, and it was already Wednesday night when Nandini checked the visit counts on her club's website. Home page: 212. Experiments page: 158. Fair sign-up page: 4.
“Four?” she messaged Leela, who ran the club's stall. “Did people not want to sign up, or not find it?”
Leela replied from the bus: “Honestly I didn't know there was a sign-up page 😅 where is it?”
Nandini looked. The link sat at the very bottom of the experiments page, below eleven photos. Nobody scrolled that far.
With the power cutting out every hour that week, she worked in bursts on her phone's battery. She put a big “Sign up for Saturday” button on the home page, second line from the top, and reposted the link in the club group.
By Friday evening the sign-up page showed 67 visits and 31 names.

qa.q: How many visits did the sign-up page have on Wednesday night?
qa.a: Four visits.

qa.q: What was Nandini thinking when the sign-up page showed only four visits?
qa.a: Nandini was puzzled and worried, unsure whether people didn't want to sign up or simply couldn't find the page 🤔

qa.q: What else could Nandini have done to learn why the page was ignored?
qa.a: Ask two or three club members to find the sign-up page while she watched, which shows the problem even faster than counts.

qa.q: What is the change like for Leela?
qa.a: Leela, who didn't even know the page existed, can now point students to a big button on the home page while running the stall.

grounding: Shows a teen seeing from visit counts that a page is ignored, asking why, moving it to the home page and checking that visits rise.

subtype: Approach: iterating from feedback and usage numbers [Revision]

Pallavi's site for Gulmohar Apartments had been running for a month: a notices page, a festival photos page, and a repair-request page she was proudest of. On Sunday she opened the simple visit counter. Notices: 340. Photos: 290. Repairs: 0.
Zero, in a building where the lift broke every other week.
She knocked on Minakshi Aunty's door on the third floor; Aunty handled repairs for the society. “Did anyone use the repair form?”
“What form?” Minakshi Aunty said. “People still ring my bell.”
Pallavi asked two more neighbours on the stairs. Neither had seen it. The link was tucked in a menu behind three lines in the corner, which most of the building's older residents never tapped.
That evening she put a big “Report a repair” box right on the home page. Two Sundays later the counter read 41, and Minakshi Aunty's bell rang a little less.

qa.a: Repairs had zero visits.

qa.a: Pallavi was probably surprised and disappointed, especially as the lift broke so often that people clearly had repairs to report.

qa.q: What else could Pallavi do so that older residents use the form?
qa.a: Put a printed notice by the lift about the box on the home page, or help a few residents try it once.

qa.q: How does the change look to Minakshi Aunty?
qa.a: For Minakshi Aunty, fewer bell rings and requests arriving in one place make the job easier.

subtype: Approach: deciding when to stop or hand over [Revision]
passage:
I'm Jeevan, from Class Nine. I help with the school quiz site that Rehana built. In December she stopped adding things. She'd been planning a leaderboard, and I asked about it twice. Both times she said, “Not before boards.”
In January she sat with me in the library for three lunch breaks. She had a thin notebook: how to add a new quiz, how to fix the answer key, who to ask if the hosting stopped. She made me do each step while she watched, not the other way round.
Then she put a line on the home page: “Paused till April for board exams. New quizzes on Mondays only, by Jeevan.” I thought she'd feel sad about it. She looked relieved, if anything, but I can't really say.
It's March now. I've added six quizzes. Nobody has complained that the site looks dead.

qa.a: How to add a new quiz, how to fix the answer key, and who to ask if the hosting stopped.

qa.a: She looked relieved rather than sad, though Jeevan admits not being sure.

qa.q: What else could Rehana have done before pausing?
qa.a: Set a short monthly check-in with Jeevan, so questions don't pile up while the site is in someone else's hands.

qa.q: What is the handover like for Jeevan?
qa.a: Jeevan gets real responsibility and a clear notebook, having practised each step, so running the site feels manageable.
